results.finding: sections, unit counts and unit forms match the spec

All 83 aligned units match the controlling idea of their spec paragraph in the spec's order (scene, argument, concepts, lasts, stressors, portable, pendulum, scorecard, debt, function, closing sections, conclusion); the five callouts carry no spec paragraph. structure.json's deterministic check also passes.

The only unit marked two_ideas (Stressor Analysis ¶5, p31) is framed by one controlling idea, 'Three things about the table matter more than any single row', with the coverage, the open-residue cluster and S1's added separation cost as its three readings, exactly as p31 declares. The S5 sentence is a subordinate note to the second reading.

Every unit serves a supporting claim: scene and concepts L2, argument L1, lasts and portable L3, stressors L4, pendulum and trade-offs L5, scorecard, debt, function and vertical L6, closing sections and conclusion several. No orphan paragraph.

Each table is introduced and read in prose (argument table by p11-p13, layers by p24-p26, families by p28, stressor table by p31, residue count by p33, portability rules by p40, sharing table by p46, scorecard by p52-p57, debt table by p49, trade-offs by p62, vertical table by p64); Figures 1-7 have explanatory captions; the Productscape and Adevinta quotations are each followed by what they show.

results.quote: [[multi-country-platforms]] describes the pendulum: groups swing between local autonomy and central platforms, and the documented record shows the swing in Schibsted's 2016 "one global product and tech organization"
results.finding: The spec declares a cause_effect transition carrying over the cost of separation (Adevinta's parallel running, end of Portability) and introducing the swing that causes such separations. The section opens by citing another chapter's description of the pendulum and re-listing the documented record; nothing at the boundary says that the swing is what produces separation costs like the one just described. The reader must infer the link from the 2025 decentralization appearing in both places. All other boundaries (sections, paragraphs, conclusion) express their declared relationship.

results.draft_locus: Setting the Scene at Veldmark: The Investor's Question ¶5
results.quote: The answer to Henrik's is the scorecard.
results.finding: The scene says the scorecard answers Henrik's question; the architecture-function section later says the 'Survivability of the record' measure, which is not on the scorecard, answers it ('Henrik's question, "what stops it from turning into another Yardstick?", is answered by this one.'). Both readers went back to the scene to work out which answer the chapter means. The spec keeps both answers deliberately (decision log: the second answers it for the record, the first for the platform), but the prose never states that distinction, so the order is fine and the prose obscures it. Reader B adds that the investor's answer is in 'The answer to the investor' subsection rather than in the stressor table the scene points to.
results.corroborated_by: flow reader A item 3a; flow reader B item 3a

results.quote: Part VIII opened with four questions: what to change first, who owns it, how you will know it worked, and what must stay true when the group's owners, laws and channels change.
results.finding: The conclusion's Part VIII closing is organised around four questions that this chapter never sets up; the chapter's own frame is one question and three moves. Both readers found the four-question frame arriving without preparation. The conclusion is required by AC-7 and p80, and neither the introduction's paragraphs nor its roadmap in the spec announce the four questions, so the difficulty comes from the spec's design rather than the prose.
results.corroborated_by: flow reader A item 3e; flow reader B item 3i

The intro reader noted the same ambiguity, but only one flow reader did. The spec's decision log kept the three-move framing as published, so the difficulty comes from the declared frame.

results.quote: Tenant codes (`hl:es`) on every identifier, event and log under Tenancy model v1
results.finding: The stressor table's S1 row names Tenancy model v1, which this chapter explains only two sections later (Portability ¶3), and the scene's list of 2027 decisions omits it. Only one reader reported it; the term comes from an earlier chapter the audience knows, so it is minor.

The does_not_know terms are defined before use: stressor analysis is glossed in the introduction and defined with stressor, attractor, residue, naive and residual architecture in Concepts (p16, p19); fitness function is defined in p20-p21 before the scorecard. Terms flagged by readers (VAS, boost archaeology, Barcelona 2027, Tenancy model v1) come from earlier chapters, which the audience already knows.
Opens with a specific, dated record (Schibsted, Adevinta, Prosus, Zillow 2016-2026) and a contrast with target-state endings, not a placeholder, restated question, definition or dawn-of-man opening.
The conclusion synthesizes Part VIII and the book, answers the opening question and hands off by contrast to Part IX; it is not a book-report recap.

p80 states the five chapters as one method and why it matters (throughput kept without the decade going to plan); p82 says what the reader gains (losses seen before a competitor's chart, fitness functions replacing milestones).

p81 restates the central claim (a liquidity machine judged by how reliably it turns fresh, trustworthy supply into matches) and the part-by-part synthesis; p82 returns to the general manager's question (smaller competitor, more contacts per listing, every team green) and matches each opening-scene loss to a fitness function.

The intro reader predicted the three moves, the section order (scene, argument, concepts, lasts, stressors, portability, pendulum, scorecard, debt, architecture function, closing sections), evidence from Schibsted/Adevinta/Prosus/Zillow and Veldmark's worked example including stressor analysis and scorecard, and a likely hand-off to Part IX. The reader noted the moves-to-sections mapping is loose (recorded under flow).

The cold reader replaced the plan with a stressor analysis across the seven families plus combined scenarios, investment in the top layer (event contract, identifiers, identity with pairwise identifiers, tenant-partitioned data, governed metrics), engines replaceable and content as data, cost to reverse with product platforms shared last, a separability estimate and yearly tenant-exit tabletop, and a dozen fitness functions with owners, counter-metrics, failure patterns and drills reviewed quarterly instead of milestones.

The reader placed the ID format in contracts and identifiers (ten years or more, new version beside old with deprecation), the search engine in engines (three to eight years, replaced behind the search contract with parallel run and parity), and package prices in content and policy (weeks to two years, released as data with experiments and review).

The reader explained that combined stressors test the decomposition (surviving by composing existing residues means it is probably right) and gave Veldmark's July 2030 scenario (sale of Hearthly Spain, generated-photo rental ring, AI assistant partner) and its finding: source-tenant provenance on the shared block list plus a tested per-tenant export of T&S cases and evidence.

p80 names the four questions, answers each with the part's chapters as one method (consolidation sequence and migration waves; one team per capability and the advice process; liquidity gates, relevance parity and the scorecard; the top-layer contracts and identifiers), which no single chapter states, and says why it matters: change sequenced this way keeps throughput without the decade going to plan.
